title: Probability — Complete Learning Module (Learn Maths with Fun)
outcomes: Define probability as P(E) = n(E)/n(S) and apply it to simple events
Distinguish between experimental and theoretical probability
Calculate probability for coin tosses, dice rolls, card draws, and ball picks
Use complementary events: P(E) + P(not E) = 1
Solve 'at least' and 'at most' probability problems
Connect probability to real-life decisions and risk assessment
Solve RD Sharma and RS Aggarwal extension problems for competitive readiness

concepts.name: Probability — The Measure of Chance
concepts.real_life_application: When the weather report says '80% chance of rain', that's probability. When a doctor says 'this surgery has a 95% success rate', that's probability. When a cricket team wins 7 out of 10 matches, the probability of winning the next match is 0.7 — until the match actually happens!
concepts.purpose: Probability quantifies uncertainty on a scale from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). It transforms 'maybe' into a precise number. It's the mathematical language of risk, used in insurance, stock markets, and medical diagnoses.
day_to_day_usage: Weather forecast: '70% chance of rain' means in 70 out of 100 similar conditions, it rained
Life insurance: premium calculated based on probability of death at a given age
Cricket: probability of winning based on historical head-to-head records
Railways: probability of a train being on time based on past data

concepts.name: Experimental vs Theoretical Probability
concepts.real_life_application: If you toss a coin 10 times and get 7 heads, the experimental probability of heads is 0.7. But theoretically, the chance is 0.5. The more tosses you do, the closer experimental probability gets to theoretical — this is the Law of Large Numbers.
concepts.purpose: Experimental probability is based on actual trials. Theoretical probability is the ideal value based on symmetry. For a fair coin, theoretical P(head) = 1/2. Experimental probability approaches this as the number of trials increases.
day_to_day_usage: A bus company tracks on-time arrivals for a year to get experimental probability
In a cricket match, the theoretical probability of heads in the toss is always 1/2
A factory tests 1000 products to find experimental probability of defects

concepts.name: Sample Space and Events
concepts.real_life_application: When you choose a card from a deck, all 52 cards form the sample space S. 'Drawing a king' is an event E with 4 favorable outcomes. P(king) = 4/52 = 1/13.
concepts.purpose: The sample space is the set of all possible outcomes. An event is a subset of the sample space. Probability = number of favorable outcomes / total number of possible outcomes. The sample space must be well-defined first.
day_to_day_usage: Rolling a die: S = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}, event 'even number' = {2, 4, 6}
Raffle draw: S = all ticket numbers, event 'win' = your ticket numbers
Traffic light: S = {red, yellow, green}, event 'stop' = {red}

concepts.name: Complementary Events
concepts.real_life_application: If the probability of passing an exam is 0.75, the probability of failing is 0.25. You either pass or fail — these are complementary events. The sum of probabilities of complementary events is always 1.
concepts.purpose: Complementary events are two events that together cover all possible outcomes and don't overlap. The complement rule P(not E) = 1 - P(E) is the most useful shortcut. Many 'at least' problems are easier when solved via complements.
day_to_day_usage: P(it rains today) + P(it doesn't rain today) = 1
'At least one head' is easier found as 1 - P(no heads)

concepts.name: Probability Problems — Dice, Coins, Cards, Balls
concepts.real_life_application: From a TV game show choosing envelopes to a lottery draw, these classic problems model real random selection. A card deck simulates any equally-likely selection problem. Dice model any uniform random number generator.
concepts.purpose: These standard problems teach the systematic counting of favorable and total outcomes. Dice: 6 outcomes. Two dice: 36 outcomes. Coin: 2 outcomes. Cards: 52 outcomes. Balls from bag: total balls = n(S). Mastering these builds intuition for complex problems.
day_to_day_usage: Card games like Teen Patti use probability to calculate winning hands
Ludo and Snakes & Ladders use a die — each number has probability 1/6
Random sampling in quality control — picking defective items from a batch

worked_examples.problem: Two unbiased coins are tossed simultaneously. Find the probability of getting: (i) at least one head, (ii) exactly one tail, (iii) at most one head.
board_mode: Given: Two coins tossed. Sample space S = {HH, HT, TH, TT}, n(S) = 4.
(i) Event E₁ 'at least one head' = {HH, HT, TH}, n(E₁) = 3
(ii) Event E₂ 'exactly one tail' = {HT, TH}, n(E₂) = 2
(iii) Event E₃ 'at most one head' = {HT, TH, TT}, n(E₃) = 3
Alternative (iii): 'At most one head' is complement of 'two heads'
P(two heads) = 1/4, so P(at most one head) = 1 - 1/4 = 3/4 ✓
worked_examples.speed_mode: Golden step: For coin problems, list all possibilities systematically. For 'at least one', use complement: 1 - P(no heads) = 1 - 1/4 = 3/4.
worked_examples.competitive_shortcut: For n coins, total outcomes = 2ⁿ. Number of outcomes with exactly r heads = ⁿCᵣ. Using combinations is faster for 3+ coins.

worked_examples.problem: Two dice are rolled simultaneously. Find the probability that the sum is 7.
worked_examples.speed_mode: Golden step: For sum problems, outcomes are symmetric. Sum 7 has 6 outcomes (the maximum for two dice). Sum 2 and 12 have 1 outcome each. Sum 6 and 8 have 5 outcomes each. Memorize the distribution.
worked_examples.competitive_shortcut: Sum distribution for two dice forms a triangle: 2(1), 3(2), 4(3), 5(4), 6(5), 7(6), 8(5), 9(4), 10(3), 11(2), 12(1). Total = 36.

worked_examples.problem: One card is drawn from a well-shuffled deck of 52 cards. Find the probability of getting: (i) a king, (ii) a red card, (iii) a face card, (iv) a black queen.
board_mode: (iii) Face cards: Jack, Queen, King per suit = 3 × 4 = 12. P(face card) = 12/52 = 3/13
(iv) Black queens: queen of spades + queen of clubs = 2. P(black queen) = 2/52 = 1/26
worked_examples.speed_mode: Golden step: Memorize the deck: 4 suits × 13 cards = 52. Suits: spades(black), hearts(red), clubs(black), diamonds(red). Each suit: Ace, 2-10, Jack, Queen, King. Face cards = J, Q, K (12 total).
worked_examples.competitive_shortcut: Ace is not a face card. Number cards = 2-10 (9 per suit = 36). Face cards = 12. Total = 36 + 12 + 4 aces = 52 ✓.

worked_examples.problem: A bag contains 5 red balls, 3 blue balls, and 2 green balls. One ball is drawn at random. Find the probability that it is: (i) red, (ii) not blue, (iii) red or green.
board_mode: (ii) Not blue = total - blue = 10 - 3 = 7. P(not blue) = 7/10 = 0.7
(iii) Red or green = 5 + 2 = 7. P(red or green) = 7/10 = 0.7
worked_examples.speed_mode: Golden step: 'Not' problems are complementary events — always check if 1 - P(E) is easier. 'Or' means add the favorable outcomes if events are mutually exclusive (can't happen together).

problems.question: Complete the statements: (i) P(E) + P(not E) = ___ (ii) Probability of an event that cannot happen is ___. (iii) Probability of an event that is certain is ___. (iv) The sum of probabilities of all elementary events is ___. (v) Probability of an event is always between ___ and ___.
A coin is tossed 1000 times with the following outcomes: Head: 455, Tail: 545. Find the experimental probability of each outcome. How does it compare with theoretical?
solution: Step 5: With 1000 tosses, experimental values are close to 0.5 but not exact. More tosses would give closer values.

problems.question: A die is thrown 1000 times. Frequencies: 1→179, 2→150, 3→157, 4→149, 5→175, 6→190. Find experimental probability of each outcome.
solution: Theoretical P(each) = 1/6 ≈ 0.167. Experimental values are close.

problems.question: Three coins are tossed simultaneously. Find the probability of getting: (i) exactly 2 heads, (ii) at least 2 heads, (iii) at most 2 tails.
solution: Step 1: Sample space for 3 coins: {HHH, HHT, HTH, HTT, THH, THT, TTH, TTT}, n(S) = 8.
Step 2 (i): Exactly 2 heads: {HHT, HTH, THH}, n = 3. P = 3/8
Step 3 (ii): At least 2 heads: {HHH, HHT, HTH, THH}, n = 4. P = 4/8 = 1/2
Step 4 (iii): At most 2 tails: complement of 3 tails (TTT). P = 1 - 1/8 = 7/8

problems.question: Two dice are rolled. Find the probability that the sum is (i) 5, (ii) 13, (iii) less than 13.
solution: Step 3 (ii): Maximum sum = 12. Sum = 13 is impossible. P = 0
Step 4 (iii): All sums are less than 13 (max 12). P = 1 (certain event)

problems.question: A box contains 90 good pens and 10 defective pens. One pen is selected at random. Find the probability that it is (i) good (ii) defective.
Two dice are rolled. Find the probability that the sum is a prime number.

topics.name: Problems with Multiple Events
topics.concept: When multiple events occur simultaneously, systematically list all combinations. Use the fundamental principle of counting: if one event has m outcomes and another has n outcomes, total combined outcomes = m × n.

examples.problem: A coin is tossed and a die is rolled simultaneously. Find the probability of getting a head and an even number.
solution: Step 1: For coin: {H, T} = 2. For die: {1,2,3,4,5,6} = 6.

topics.competitive_note: Multiple-event problems are the foundation for complex probability in JEE (Class XI/XII). Master the counting principle here.

topics.name: Cards — Full Deck Analysis
topics.concept: A standard deck: 52 cards, 4 suits (♠♣♥♦), 13 cards per suit. Face cards: J, Q, K (12 total). Aces: 4. Number cards: 2-10 (36 total).
topics.competitive_note: Memorize the deck structure. Common problems: 'red face card' (6/52), 'black ace' (2/52), 'king or queen' (8/52).

topics.name: 'At Least' and 'At Most' Problems
topics.concept: Use complement for 'at least' problems: P(at least one) = 1 - P(none). For 'at most', count directly or use complement.

examples.problem: Two dice are rolled. Find the probability of getting at least one 6.
solution: Step 2: P(no 6 on first die) = 5/6, P(no 6 on second) = 5/6

topics.name: Drawing Without Replacement
topics.concept: When drawing two items without replacement, the sample space changes after the first draw. The probability for the second draw depends on the first outcome.
topics.competitive_note: This is a bridge to conditional probability (Class XII). Practice these to build intuition for dependent events.

Card problems — memorize the deck structure

common_mistakes: Counting (1,1) only once when two dice are rolled — both dice are distinct, so (1,1) is one of 36 ordered pairs
Forgetting that Ace is not a face card
Using 'or' when events are mutually exclusive vs not — in Class X, all given events are mutually exclusive
Calculation errors in total outcomes for three coins (always 8, not 6)

simple.question: The probability of a certain event is:
simple.explanation: A certain event always happens, so its probability is 1.

simple.question: When a coin is tossed, P(head) = ?
simple.explanation: A fair coin has two equally likely outcomes: head and tail. P(head) = 1/2.

simple.question: Total outcomes when two dice are rolled:
simple.explanation: Each die has 6 outcomes, so total = 6 × 6 = 36.

simple.question: P(E) + P(not E) = ?
simple.explanation: E and not E are complementary — they cover all possibilities. So P(E) + P(not E) = 1.

simple.question: How many face cards are in a deck of 52?
simple.explanation: Each suit has 3 face cards (Jack, Queen, King). 4 suits × 3 = 12 face cards.

vedic_math_shortcuts.title: Vedic Method: Sample Space Counting Using Urdhva Tiryagbhyam
vedic_math_shortcuts.concept: 'Urdhva Tiryagbhyam' (Vertically and Crosswise) — the most versatile Vedic sutra. Used here for systematic counting: when combining two independent events (coin + coin, coin + die, two dice), multiply outcomes vertically for total sample space.
vedic_math_shortcuts.real_numbers_application: For 2 coins: 2 × 2 = 4 outcomes. For 3 coins: 2 × 2 × 2 = 8. For 2 dice: 6 × 6 = 36. For coin + die: 2 × 6 = 12. Visualize as a grid — vertically one set, crosswise the other.

examples.problem: Two dice and a coin are tossed together. Total outcomes?
steps: Vedic: Urdhva Tiryagbhyam — multiply vertically and crosswise.
examples.regular_method: Same multiplication, but Vedic presentation makes it intuitive as a vertical-crisscross grid.

vedic_math_shortcuts.title: Vedic Method: Complementary Events Using Anurupye (Proportion)
vedic_math_shortcuts.concept: 'Anurupye' (Proportionality) — if P(E) is known, P(not E) follows by complement. The sum of all probabilities is 1 = total. This is proportionality in its simplest form.
vedic_math_shortcuts.real_numbers_application: P(at least one) = 1 - P(none). This Vedic insight avoids counting complex favorable cases directly.

examples.problem: Three coins tossed. Find P(at least one head).
steps: Vedic Anurupye: P(at least one) = 1 - P(no heads).
Compare: directly counting would need 7 favorable cases — slower.
examples.regular_method: Count {HHH, HHT, HTH, HTT, THH, THT, TTH} = 7/8. Vedic method is faster.

vedic_math_shortcuts.title: Vedic Method: Card Probability By Memory Bandhas
vedic_math_shortcuts.concept: 'Bandhas' (Structural binding) — memorize the deck structure as a fixed pattern: 4 suits × 13 cards = 52. Each suit: A, 2-10, J, Q, K. Face cards = J+Q+K = 3 per suit × 4 = 12. This structure is a 'bandha' (fixed pattern) that never changes.
vedic_math_shortcuts.real_numbers_application: Once the deck structure is memorized, any card probability can be computed instantly without listing all cards.

steps: Vedic Bandha: Face cards = 12. Red suits = 2 (hearts, diamonds).
examples.regular_method: Same calculation, but Vedic approach emphasizes structural pattern recognition.

steps: Vedic Bandha: Kings = 4, Red cards = 26, Red kings counted twice.
examples.regular_method: Same formula, but Vedic method visualizes as set intersection.

vedic_math_shortcuts.title: Vedic Method: Dice Sum Distribution Using Meru Prastara
vedic_math_shortcuts.concept: 'Meru Prastara' (Pascal's triangle/Meru mountain) — the sum distribution for two dice follows the triangular pattern: 1,2,3,4,5,6,5,4,3,2,1 for sums 2 through 12. This is the Meru sequence, known to Vedic mathematicians long before Pascal.
vedic_math_shortcuts.real_numbers_application: P(sum=7) = 6/36 = 1/6 (peak of the triangle). P(sum=2 or 12) = 1/36 each (ends). The entire distribution is symmetric.

examples.problem: Two dice rolled. P(sum = 5) vs P(sum = 9) — are they equal?
steps: Vedic Meru: The distribution is symmetric about 7.
Sum 5 is 2 below 7, Sum 9 is 2 above 7. They are symmetric.

common_misconceptions: Students think probability can be greater than 1 or negative. Probability is always between 0 and 1 inclusive.
Students think experimental probability is 'wrong' if it differs from theoretical. Experimental approaches theoretical as trials increase (Law of Large Numbers) but is not 'wrong'.
Students list only 3 outcomes for 2 coins (HH, HT, TT) instead of 4 (HH, HT, TH, TT). The two coins are distinct — HT and TH are different outcomes.
Students forget that Ace is NOT a face card. Face cards are J, Q, K only (12 total). Ace is a number card in probability.
Students think the probability of a 6 on a die is 'either happens or not, so 1/2'. This is the 'Fair doesn't mean 50-50' fallacy. Outcomes must be equally likely, not binary.
Students use P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) without checking for overlap. In Class X, events given are mutually exclusive, but students should still verify.
Students think drawing without replacement keeps probabilities the same. After removing one ball, the total changes and probabilities update.
Students answer 'at least one' problems by listing all favorable cases instead of using the complement. For large n, listing is impractical — always use 1 - P(none).

sub_nodes: Experimental: based on actual trials (observed frequency)
Law of Large Numbers: experimental → theoretical as trials ↑
Both are valid — context determines which to use
3 coins: 8 outcomes — use combinations for speed
Product/prime sum problems require systematic listing
Face cards: J, Q, K = 12 total
Ace is NOT a face card

flowcharts.title: How to Solve Any Probability Problem

steps.action: Identify the experiment (coin, dice, cards, balls, etc.)
Determine total outcomes n(S) by counting or multiplication principle
Define the event E clearly — what outcomes are favorable?
Does the problem say 'at least' or 'at most'?
Use complement: P(at least) = 1 - P(none). P(at most) = sum of individual cases or complement.
Count favorable outcomes n(E) directly (list, multiply, or use combinations)
Simplify fraction to lowest terms. Check: 0 ≤ P ≤ 1. Verify with complement.
Total: 52 cards. 4 suits × 13 ranks per suit.
Black suits: ♠ spades (13), ♣ clubs (13). Red suits: ♥ hearts (13), ♦ diamonds (13).
Face cards: J, Q, K (3 per suit × 4 = 12 total). Ace is NOT face card.
Probability questions combine: color + rank + suit. E.g., 'red king' → 2 cards out of 52.
For 'or' questions: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B). Avoid double-counting.
